aiExplanation: This solution finds the level of a binary tree with the **largest sum of node values** using an iterative **breadth-first search** (level-order traversal). It keeps the current level's nodes in `stack` and, on each pass of the `while` loop, adds up all their values into `sum` while collecting their children into a `next` array for the following level. After summing a level, it compares `sum` against the best seen so far (`max`, initialized to `-Infinity` so even all-negative levels work): if the new sum is larger, it records both the sum and the level number in `maxLevel`. It then replaces `stack` with `next`, increments `level`, and repeats until there are no more nodes, finally returning the **smallest level with the maximum sum** since only strictly greater sums replace the record.

author: Vitor
aiExplanation: This solution uses a recursive **depth-first search** to total up the node values on each level of the tree. The `dfs` helper walks the tree while tracking the current `level`, and a `Map` accumulates the running sum per level via `map.set(level, (map.get(level) || 0) + node.val)`. After the traversal, a `while` loop walks levels `1, 2, 3, ...` in order, tracking the biggest sum in `max` and the level where it occurred in `maxLvl`, then returns that level. The subtle flaw here is that `max` starts at `0` instead of `-Infinity`: if **every level has a negative sum**, no level ever beats `0`, so the function incorrectly falls back to returning level `1` — which is why this attempt failed.

author: Vitor
aiExplanation: This solution finds the tree level with the **largest sum of node values** in two phases. First, a recursive **depth-first search** (`dfs`) visits every node while carrying its `level` (starting at `1` for the root), and a `Map` keeps a running total per level — the expression `(map.get(level) || 0) + node.val` adds each node's value to its level's sum, defaulting to `0` the first time a level is seen. Second, a `while` loop scans the levels in ascending order using `map.has(level)`, updating `max` and `maxLvl` whenever a level's sum is **strictly greater** than the best so far, which guarantees the smallest such level wins ties. Crucially, `max` starts at `-Infinity`, so the comparison works correctly even when **all level sums are negative** — the fix that makes this attempt pass where the previous one failed.
